content:
Claude Code's auto mode will become the default permission setting for users next week.

Starting August 14, conversations for Pro, Max, and Team users will use auto mode by default, unless users or administrators have pinned other settings.

Anthropic will no longer charge for the additional tokens generated by each tool call from the auto mode classifier.

According to Anthropic, auto mode replaces repetitive approval prompts with a classifier that checks each tool call for irreversible, destructive, or out-of-scope actions.

If the classifier blocks an action, Claude can attempt a safer alternative or request authorization. After multiple blocks, the conversation will fall back to manual approval mode.

As part of this adjustment, Anthropic said it will no longer charge for the "small amount of additional tokens" generated by each tool call from the auto mode classifier.

Anthropic pointed out that its research on 1,053 paid testers found that humans could only identify 13.6% of dangerous instructions, while auto mode could identify 89%. After 50 prompts, human performance dropped further to about 5%.

However, Anthropic still reminds that the classifier cannot completely eliminate risks and recommends manual review when making changes to production environments.

This change should help Claude Code handle long-duration tasks, combined with routine procedures, voice mode, and the built-in Mac browser in the application. Anthropic said that Team and Enterprise customers' auto mode users submitted about 25% more pull requests.

9to5Mac commentary

Although it sounds risky, for experienced users, this should be a reasonable default setting. However, users should still establish a certain level of trust with the coding agent before relying on auto mode.

Anthropic's taking this step is also quite thought-provoking. For comparison, OpenAI once chose to turn off auto mode for its most powerful GPT-5.6 version as an additional safeguard.
